- **WHEN** `markerVisibility` is `'all'` and a document contains a heading, paragraph, code
  fence, table, callout, quote, HTML block, and horizontal rule
- **THEN** each renders its own kind-specific marker on its first line, and none render on
  any continuation or gap line

#### Scenario: List items are unchanged
- **WHEN** a list item is rendered in outline mode, at any `markerVisibility` setting
- **THEN** it shows Obsidian's native bullet/number exactly as it would outside outline
  mode, with no additional synthetic marker

#### Scenario: 'with-children' hides leaf markers, including atoms
- **WHEN** `markerVisibility` is `'with-children'`
- **THEN** only nodes with at least one child render a marker; every atom (leaf by
  construction) renders none, regardless of kind

#### Scenario: 'headings-and-paragraphs' keys off kind, not instance state
- **WHEN** `markerVisibility` is `'headings-and-paragraphs'`
- **THEN** every heading and paragraph renders a marker whether or not it currently has
  children, and no atom kind ever renders one

#### Scenario: Hiding a marker never reflows text
- **WHEN** `markerVisibility` changes such that a previously-visible marker is hidden
- **THEN** the line's indentation (padding-left/margin-left) is unchanged; only the marker
  icon's presence changes

#### Scenario: Marker setting changes take effect without a rebuild
- **WHEN** `markerVisibility` is changed while a note is open in outline mode
- **THEN** the next render reflects the new setting, including for widget-replaced atoms
  whose decoration output would otherwise be byte-identical across the change

**Covered by**: `tests/decorate.test.ts` ("marks only the first line of each node as
isFirstLine", "flags hasNativeMarker only for list-item first lines", "carries the node
kind at every line, including list-item continuations", "carries whether the node has
children, constant across its own lines"); `e2e/specs/52-block-markers-icons.e2e.ts`

line only", "widget-replaced atom kinds (table/callout/html/hr) each get exactly one marker
child", "list items get no marker at all (native bullet/number only)", "marker doesn't
repeat/duplicate across a live document edit (idempotent DOM patch)", "multi-line
continuation: a code fence's marker sits only on the opener line, indentation stays
consistent across all its lines", "'with-children': only branch nodes get a marker,
regardless of kind", "'with-children': a widget-replaced atom (table) with children
obviously still gets no marker — atoms are always leaves", "'headings-and-paragraphs': only
those two kinds get a marker, leaf or not — atoms never do", "changing marker visibility
live (no rebuild) toggles a leaf marker on the very next edit", "hiding a marker never
reflows the reserved gutter — text position is unaffected").

### Requirement: Markers are fixed-size and coexist with native and guide chrome
A marker's size SHALL be a fixed length (never `em`, which would resolve against the
surrounding line's own font-size), identical across every kind and heading level. A marker
SHALL NOT remove, replace, or visibly collide with Obsidian's native blockquote bar, the
CSS containment/specificity rules widget atoms carry, or Obsidian's native fold chevron on a
heading.

#### Scenario: Marker size is font-size-independent
- **WHEN** a marker renders on a heading line and on a paragraph line
- **THEN** its rendered width and height are identical despite the heading's larger font

#### Scenario: Blockquote native bar and marker coexist
- **WHEN** a blockquote line also carries a marker
- **THEN** both Obsidian's native colored bar and the marker render, neither clobbering the
  other

#### Scenario: A depth-0 widget atom's marker is not clipped
- **WHEN** a table with no ancestor (tree depth 0) renders a marker
- **THEN** the marker is fully visible, not clipped by Obsidian's native `contain: paint`
  containment

#### Scenario: Fold chevron stays clear of the marker and any active guide
- **WHEN** a heading has a foldable child, so Obsidian renders its native fold chevron
- **THEN** the chevron does not overlap the heading's own marker or an ancestor's guide
  line passing through the same row

**Covered by**: `e2e/specs/52-block-markers-icons.e2e.ts` ("blockquote: native colored bar
and the marker widget coexist (DOM widget, not a pseudo-element — no clobber by
construction)", "marker size is fixed (rem), NOT font-size-dependent — identical
width/height on a heading vs. a paragraph line", "no !important/specificity or
contain:paint regression: a depth-0 table (no ancestor guide) still shows its marker
unclipped", "code fence and blockquote markers align horizontally with a same-depth
paragraph's (native padding/text-indent compensation)", "heading marker vertical offset
from the line's own center is small and doesn't grow with heading level (H1 vs H3)",
"native fold chevron glyph sits between the marker and an ancestor's guide line, clear of
both").

### Requirement: Nested per-cell editors receive no decorations
Obsidian renders an actively-edited table cell in Live Preview as its own independent CM6
editor instance mounted inside the outer table widget's DOM. This nested editor's own
"document" (the cell's raw text) SHALL receive no indentation, no guide, and no marker,
even though its outline-mode gate resolves to the same file as the real top-level note.

#### Scenario: Editing a table cell does not decorate the cell's own text
- **WHEN** a table cell in an outline-mode note is actively being edited
- **THEN** the cell's own nested editor renders with no added padding/margin and no marker,
  regardless of what the cell's raw text would otherwise parse as

**Covered by**: `e2e/specs/53-decoration-contracts.e2e.ts` ("a nested per-cell table
editor carries no decoration state at all (isNestedEditor gate)" — opens a cell for
editing and asserts, via computed styles, zero padding/margin/marker on the nested
editor's own line while the outer note's decorations stay active). The requirement was
originally surfaced indirectly by a flaky marker-visibility test traced to this exact
leak — see
[docs/research/10-experiment-5-block-markers.md](../../../docs/research/10-experiment-5-block-markers.md#follow-up-round-4-a-genuine-architectural-bug-found-via-a-flaky-test--decorations-leaking-into-obsidians-own-nested-per-cell-editors).

### Requirement: Decorations never mutate document state
The decoration layer SHALL be a pure rendering projection: it SHALL NOT dispatch any
document-changing transaction, move the cursor/selection, or create undo history entries,
regardless of how often it recomputes.

#### Scenario: Rendering produces no transaction
- **WHEN** the decoration layer recomputes after a document change
- **THEN** no new transaction is dispatched beyond the one that triggered the recompute,
  and the document text, cursor position, and undo stack are exactly as they were left by
  that triggering change

**Covered by**: `e2e/specs/53-decoration-contracts.e2e.ts` ("a decoration recompute
mutates nothing: buffer, cursor, and undo stack all unchanged" — after a known real edit,
a double mode toggle leaves buffer and cursor byte-identical, and a single undo reverts
that edit, proving no change-bearing transaction was interposed); `tests/decorate.test.ts`
("produces no facts for an empty document or preamble-only document" — the pure
computation has no side effects to begin with).

### Requirement: Widget-replaced lines receive indentation, markers, and guides via direct DOM patching
Obsidian replaces some lines in Live Preview with opaque elements on which a CM6
`Decoration.line` has no effect. Which lines those are SHALL NOT be assumed to correspond to
any set of node kinds, NOR SHALL they be identified by enumerating the CSS classes those
elements happen to carry: tables, callouts, raw HTML blocks, and horizontal rules are always
widget-replaced, but a line of ANY kind can be — a paragraph consisting of a note embed
(`![[Another note]]`) is one, and an embed can also occupy one line of a multi-line node or
a list item's line. A line-level replacement SHALL be recognized structurally, by standing
in for a whole editor line, so that a widget-rendered kind the layer has never seen is
handled correctly by construction.

Every line that Obsidian replaces with an opaque widget SHALL receive its indentation
contribution, its marker, its ancestors' guides, and its selection chrome via direct DOM
patching (inline styles and an injected marker child element) applied after each render,
computed from THAT LINE's own decoration facts — its depth, kind, first-line status, and
list-item status — exactly as the corresponding plain `.cm-line` would have received them.
The marker SHALL therefore follow the line's node kind: a widget-replaced paragraph line
renders the paragraph marker, a widget-replaced list-item line renders none (its native
bullet/number is untouched), and a widget-replaced continuation line renders none.

Native padding the widget itself contributes SHALL be read live (never hardcoded) and
subtracted so the widget's visible content aligns with same-depth content of other kinds,
clamped so a depth-0 line's contribution never goes negative.

A line MAY be rendered by two elements at once: with the cursor on it, Obsidian can reveal
the raw source as its own `.cm-line` while KEEPING the rendered element. Both SHALL carry
the line's indentation, so the two stay aligned, but the line SHALL render exactly ONE
marker — the declarative one on the source line, with the widget suppressing its own
whenever a declarative marker exists for that line and has a `.cm-line` to render on.

A widget nested INSIDE a rendered `.cm-line` (for example an inline image embed among a
paragraph's text) SHALL NOT be patched: its host line is a real `.cm-line` that already
received its decoration declaratively, and patching the nested element too would shift it a
second time. Only a widget standing in for a whole editor line SHALL be patched. Cleanup —
removing a previously applied patch — SHALL be confined to widgets that genuinely carry no
line-level decoration state, and SHALL NOT be reached merely because a widget-replaced
line's node is not an atom.

#### Scenario: Widget atoms indent like plain atoms
- **WHEN** a table, callout, HTML block, or horizontal rule sits at a non-zero tree depth
- **THEN** its rendered position matches a same-depth code block or callout, not offset by
  its own native internal padding

#### Scenario: A widget-replaced non-atom line is decorated, not skipped
- **WHEN** a paragraph consisting of a note embed sits at a non-zero tree depth and renders
  as an opaque replacement element
- **THEN** it carries the paragraph's own indentation contribution, its paragraph marker,
  and every guide its ancestors own — not a flush-left undecorated block

#### Scenario: A widget-replaced continuation line takes its node's indentation and no marker
- **WHEN** a note embed occupies one line of a multi-line paragraph, so that line is
  widget-replaced while the node's first line is not
- **THEN** it carries the same indentation contribution as the node's first line, and no
  marker of its own

#### Scenario: A list-item line keeps native list rendering whatever it contains
- **WHEN** a list item's line contains a note embed (e.g. `- ![[Another note]]`)
- **THEN** it receives its `supplementalDepth` contribution and no synthetic marker, exactly
  as a list item containing only text does

#### Scenario: A doubly rendered line shows one marker, not two
- **WHEN** the cursor is on a note-embed paragraph line, so Obsidian renders both the raw
  source as a `.cm-line` and the embed block for that same line
- **THEN** exactly one marker renders for the line, and both elements start at the same
  column

#### Scenario: A widget nested inside a rendered line is left alone
- **WHEN** a paragraph line contains an inline embed among other text, so the line renders
  as a real `.cm-line` with a widget element nested inside it
- **THEN** the line's own indentation and marker render once, from the line's declarative
  decoration, and the nested widget receives no patch of its own — no doubled shift

**Covered by**: `e2e/specs/50-decorations.e2e.ts` ("widget-replaced atoms (table, callout,

plus `e2e/specs/54-widget-rendered-lines.e2e.ts`, which covers each placement an embed can
occupy (whole-paragraph line, one line of a multi-line node, list-item line, inline among
text) with the cursor parked away from them, and separately covers the cursor-on state for
the whole-paragraph case — where Obsidian renders the source line and the embed block at
once, and only one of the two may carry a marker.

### Requirement: A provisional position renders as the node it would become

A PROVISIONAL POSITION (`outline-keyboard-grammar`) is a line the caret rests on that carries
no node content of its own — a blank or whitespace-only line the parse assigns to a node's
trailing gap. While the primary selection is a single empty cursor on such a line, and the
line belongs to a node's gap rather than to the document preamble, that line SHALL take its
INDENTATION AND MARKER facts from the line the document's own parse would produce there if a
character were typed at the caret: the same indentation regime (block padding, atom/list
margin), the same depth or `supplementalDepth`, the same node kind, and the same marker

/*
 * Outline mode decorations — additive-only indentation (Experiment 1, see
 * docs/research/08-experiment-1-additive-indentation.md and the postmortem
 * it links). `rem`, not `em`: custom properties resolve at the point of use,
 * so an `em`-based unit would inflate under a heading's larger font-size —
 * exactly the bug that shipped last time.
 *
 * Selector specificity: `!important` alone is not enough. Obsidian's own
 * app.css has `.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content > * { margin: 0px
 * !important; }` (three classes) resetting margin on every `.cm-line` —
 * our `.cm-line.to-decor-*` (two classes) lost to it outright even with
 * `!important` on both sides, confirmed live against a real build. Matching
 * the same ancestor structure they use is what wins the cascade, not the
 * `!important` keyword by itself.
 */

/*
 * `--to-marker-gutter` (Experiment 5a, see
 * docs/research/10-experiment-5-block-markers.md): a fixed, additive
 * reservation for a per-kind block marker icon, on top of the existing
 * depth-based indentation. Applies to every non-list-item line (block and
 * atom alike) — list items reserve nothing, since they keep their fully
 * native marker untouched. `rem`, never `em`, same reasoning as
 * `--to-decor-unit` above. Explicitly set per-line by `lineDecoration()`
 * (decorations.ts) — this rule's own fallback (`0px`) only matters before
 * that JS has run at all; it is never the value actually in effect.
 * `position: relative` gives the marker icon
 * (a real, absolutely-positioned DOM child, not a pseudo-element — the
 * whole reason Experiment 5a doesn't need to fight over `::before`/
 * `::after` with the guide or blockquote's native bar) a containing block
 * matching this line's own box.
 */
.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content > .cm-line.to-decor-block {
  position: relative;
  padding-left: calc(
    var(--to-depth, 0) * var(--to-decor-unit, 1.5rem) + var(--to-marker-gutter, 0px)
  ) !important;
  /* Headings/paragraphs whose raw line starts with 1-3 literal spaces (not
   * enough to reclassify as an indented code block) get a native HyperMD
   * "hang" from Obsidian: a `padding-inline-start`/`text-indent` pair meant
   * to keep soft-wrapped continuation lines aligned under the first visible
   * character. Our own `padding-left` above always wins that fight (`!important`
   * beats a non-important inline style even across the logical/physical
   * property pair, confirmed live) — but `text-indent` is never touched by
   * us at all, so its native negative value (which Obsidian derives from a
   * measurement taken AFTER our own padding has already shifted the box,
   * confirmed live: for a single leading space the observed value wasn't
   * ~4px, the width of one space, but ~4px + our own padding-left, i.e. it
   * double-counts our own contribution) leaks straight through unopposed.
   * Net first-line shift becomes `ourPadding - nativeTextIndent`, which is
   * NEGATIVE — outdented past the depth column, growing with every extra
   * leading space (more native "measured" width to subtract), exactly the
   * reported bug. Zeroing text-indent removes the hang outright: the line
   * renders purely at our own depth position, and the literal leading
   * spaces still show up as ordinary rendered content on top of it (additive
   * -only, same invariant every other kind here already keeps) instead of
   * being folded into a hanging-indent calculation that assumes zero prior
   * padding. */
  text-indent: 0 !important;
}

/* Atoms (code/table/quote/callout/html/hr) render a visible background or
 * border box; padding-left only shifts an element's own content, never
 * that box, so atoms need margin-left instead. */
.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content > .cm-line.to-decor-atom {
  position: relative;
  margin-left: calc(
    var(--to-depth, 0) * var(--to-decor-unit, 1.5rem) + var(--to-marker-gutter, 0px)
  ) !important;
}

/* List items: native text-indent/padding-left (the bullet hang) is never
 * touched. margin-left is a box-model property native list rendering
 * doesn't otherwise use, so adding supplemental depth here is genuinely
 * additive on top of untouched native positioning. */
.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content > .cm-line.to-decor-list {
  margin-left: calc(var(--to-supp-depth, 0) * var(--to-decor-unit, 1.5rem)) !important;
}

/*
 * Guide lines (Experiment 2b) — CSS stacked-gradient technique
 * (@replit/codemirror-indentation-markers), see
 * docs/research/09-experiment-2-guide-lines.md. decorations.ts merges a
 * `--to-guides` custom property (a comma-joined list of repeating-linear-
 * gradient layers, one per active ancestor depth) into the same line that
 * already carries `--to-depth`/`--to-supp-depth` — a single `::before`
 * renders every layer as one background, O(1) DOM nodes regardless of
 * depth, on every kind (block, atom, list item, AND widget-replaced atoms
 * — table/callout/hr/html — which AtomWidgetMargins patches directly via
 * the same class/custom-properties, since a `Decoration.line` has no
 * effect on those at all, same as its margin-left compensation).
 *
 * `to-decor-atom`/`to-decor-list` lines use `margin-left`, which shifts
 * the LINE'S OWN BOX — an early version of this code assumed that meant a
 * guide could never render on those lines at all (a background confined
 * to match the line's own box would indeed be stuck there). That was
 * wrong: a pseudo-element's own box does NOT have to match its containing
 * block's dimensions. `left` here widens the pseudo leftward by exactly
 * `--to-own-shift` — the line's own fully-known margin-left shift — so
 * its box starts at the SAME global column regardless of which kind of
 * line it's on, and `background-position` inside decorations.ts's
 * gradient layers then lands each guide at the correct absolute column.
 * Confirmed live that nothing between a plain `.cm-line` and
 * `.cm-scroller` clips this leftward overflow.
 *
 * Neither `!important` nor Obsidian's own ancestor-chain specificity
 * workaround is needed for `position`/`background` themselves (unlike
 * padding-left/margin-left above): those aren't contested by any of
 * Obsidian's own rules on the elements this targets — confirmed live.
 *
 * Matched on OUR OWN class alone (`> .to-decor-guides`), with no Obsidian
 * class qualifying it. An earlier version wrote out
 * `> .cm-line.to-decor-guides, > .cm-embed-block.to-decor-guides`, which
 * silently meant "plain lines and the atom kinds" — a wiki embed carries
 * neither class, so its guide class was set by the ViewPlugin and then
 * matched nothing at all (measured: the element had `to-decor-guides` and a
 * resolved `::after` background of `none`). Since we only ever set this
 * class on an element that renders a whole line, the direct-child
 * combinator alone already says everything that needs saying, and it stays
 * true for whatever Obsidian widget-renders next. Same reasoning applies to
 * the `.to-decor-node-selected` rules below.
 *
 * Uses `::after`, not `::before`: Obsidian implements a blockquote's own
 * colored side-bar via a NATIVE `::before` (`border-left`, `position:
 * absolute; left: 0`, confirmed live via computed style with outline mode
 * off) — an early version of this rule used `::before` too, which doesn't
 * "double up" with the native one, it completely REPLACES it (an element
 * has exactly one `::before`), silently deleting the native bar wherever
 * a guide became active on a blockquote line. Confirmed `::after` is
 * unused (`content: none`) by every kind this rule targets, including all
 * four widget kinds, before switching to it.
 */
.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content > .to-decor-guides {
  position: relative;
}

.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content > .to-decor-guides::after {
  content: '';
  position: absolute;
  top: 0;
  left: calc(-1 * var(--to-own-shift, 0px));
  right: 0;
  bottom: 0;
  background: var(--to-guides);
  pointer-events: none;
  z-index: -1;
}

/*
 * Position indicators (hierarchy-position-indicators): the caret-derived
 * accents share the `::after` overlay above, riding in the SAME
 * comma-separated background list as the guides (decorations.ts's
 * `guideBackground`) — the only place left, since `::before` is spoken for
 * twice over and a plain `.cm-line` cannot take a real DOM child.
 *
 * That sharing is why the guide overlay above no longer carries a flat
 * `opacity: 0.6`: one opacity on the pseudo-element would dim the accent
 * along with the base guides, and there is no second pseudo to separate
 * them onto. The dimming moved into the guide's own color instead, which is
 * equivalent here (a single, non-overlapping layer composited against the
 * page) and leaves the accent free to render at full strength.
 *
 * Both accent variables resolve from the active theme, so a snippet can
 * retune color and weight with no plugin setting and no geometry change —
 * the theming pattern docs/research/12 recommends, and the same pair
 * Logseq's own bullet_threading.css exposes.
 */
.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content {
  --to-guide-color: color-mix(in srgb, var(--text-faint) 60%, transparent);
  --to-decor-accent: var(--text-accent);
  /* Same width as an unaccented guide (`guideLayer`'s own 1px), so an accent is
   * purely a change of color: the line does not thicken as the caret moves into

   * unaccented one did. A heavier value reads as emphasis-by-weight and makes
   * the accented column visibly jump; retune with a snippet if that is wanted. */
  --to-trail-width: 1px;
}

66-  `content` on `.cm-indent::before` renders — no specificity fight, no containment problem.
67-  The native `::before` is already `position: absolute` with a zero-width-space `content`, so
68-  the hook is real rather than something we have to construct.
69-- **Obsidian's own guide column is not where a trail segment wants to draw.** The native `::before`
70-  computes to `left: 36px` — the span's *right* edge, i.e. `84 + 36k` absolutely — while the
71-  ancestor bullet that a trail segment should descend from sits at `60 + 36k`. The offset
72-  between them is constant (`12px` here: the bullet's own offset inside its level's slot), but
73-  it is a theme-dependent metric, not a constant to hardcode — the same trap `nativeMarginBasePx`
74-  and the table widget's native padding already taught this codebase to measure rather than
75-  assume.
76-
77-Also worth recording: with `showIndentGuide: true`, the bundled theme's `.cm-indent::before`
78-computes to `border-left: 0px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)` — the native indent guide draws nothing here.

80-own line, merely positioned by native geometry.

85-since span `k` would be list level `k`. A second probe, measuring several indentation styles,
86-shows that assumption is wrong twice over.

89-
90-| markdown indentation | bullet columns | `.cm-indent` spans per line |
91-| -------------------- | -------------- | --------------------------- |
92-| 4 spaces             | 12, 48, 84     | 0, 1, 2                     |
93-| tab                  | 12, 48, 84     | 0, 1, 2                     |
94-| 2 spaces             | 12, 20, 48     | 0, **0**, 1                 |

98-- **`.cm-indent` count is not the list level.** With 2-space indentation a genuine level-2 item

content.content:
# Obsidian Plugin Landscape

What exists today, how each plugin works internally, and where the gaps are.
(Internals verified against source via DeepWiki, July 2026.)

## Editing-side plugins

### [obsidian-outliner](https://github.com/vslinko/obsidian-outliner) (vslinko)

The incumbent, and the baseline to improve upon.

**How it works.** A features/services architecture on top of official APIs:
`registerEditorExtension` with CodeMirror 6 keymaps at `Prec.highest` (Enter, Tab), an
`EditorState.transactionExtender` that keeps the cursor inside list content and out of folded
regions ("stick cursor"), CM6 extensions for drag-and-drop and vertical indent lines, and its
own markdown list parser + operation engine (`Parser`, `OperationPerformer`) working through a
`MyEditor` wrapper. Mostly clean API usage; the exceptions are `(editor as any).cm` to reach the
CM6 `EditorView` (ubiquitous community pattern, not in public typings) and
`window.CodeMirrorAdapter.Vim` for vim `o`/`O` support.

**What it delivers**: move-with-children, indent/outdent, folding shortcuts, smarter
Enter/Tab, Ctrl+A escalation (item → whole list), drag-and-drop, indent guides, list styling.

**Where it falls short of a true outliner** (the motivating gaps for this project):

- **No structure enforcement.** It's "a flat text with cursor tricks bolted on top" — nothing
  stops a newline from starting flat paragraph text next to the outline; nothing validates the
  tree.
- **No node-level selection model.** Selections are raw text spans; the README itself lists
  *"manipulation with multiple lines"* as not supported. A careless select-and-delete still
  shreds structure and leaves broken indentation.
- No zoom (delegated to the companion plugin), no node identity, no references/mirrors,
  no structured backlinks — it is purely a list-editing enhancer.
- 95 open issues; maintained but conservative in scope (v4.10.2, June 2026).

### [obsidian-zoom](https://github.com/vslinko/obsidian-zoom) (vslinko)

Zoom into a list subtree. **How it works**: a CM6 `StateField` dispatching effects that create
`Decoration.replace({block: true})` decorations hiding everything outside the zoomed range, a
`transactionFilter` limiting selection to the visible range, and a breadcrumbs header. Public
APIs only. Requires "Fold heading"/"Fold indent" enabled. Proves **zoom/hoisting is achievable
with pure public-API CM6** in the standard markdown view.

### [obsidian-pro-outliner](https://github.com/mrkhachaturov/obsidian-pro-outliner) (mrkhachaturov)

A 2025 unification-fork of outliner + zoom (MIT, credits vslinko) that pushes furthest toward
the true-outliner UX and is therefore an important precedent:

- Zoom with **compact breadcrumbs** and zoom-out-one-level;
- **Mirrors** — Tana-style synced copies of blocks across notes (one-way sync, dashed-bullet
  indicator, break-link command; only top-level items mirrorable, nested items fall back to
  block links);
- **Workflowy-style selection expansion** — selections crossing bullets auto-expand to whole
  items with children.

Young (v1.0.6, Dec 2025, 21 stars), but demonstrates that node selection, mirrors, and
breadcrumbed zoom are all buildable inside the markdown view.

### [bullet](https://github.com/kdnk/obsidian-bullet) (kdnk)

Active fork of obsidian-outliner (v5.5.9, ~monthly releases) with vim-mode integration and
cursor-positioning tweaks. Scorecard on the community directory: Health "Excellent."
No fundamental additions over the parent — same flat-text limitations.

### draggable-list-items

Subsumed: obsidian-outliner (and pro-outliner) ship drag-and-drop natively.

### [workflowy-style-outline](https://github.com/springrain1/workflowy-style-outline) (springrain1) — the Option B case study

*(Added 2026-07-13 — reviewed after the architecture decisions; it independently attempts our
"mode toggle + md↔outline conversion" idea via the custom-view route, so it doubles as a field
test of the road we didn't take.)*

**What it is.** A Workflowy-style block editor for markdown notes (v2.9.1, ~10k lines,
squash-committed as a "fix all Obsidian review issues" clean drop; README additionally
advertises license-gated features not present in this snapshot). Rich feature set: per-note
toggle to an outline view, zoom + breadcrumbs, multi-selection, drag-and-drop (Alt+drag creates
block references with auto-generated native `^block-id`s), slash/tag/link suggestion menus,
todo states, mobile toolbar.

**How it works** (verified in source):

- `WorkflowyView extends FileView` — a **from-scratch block editor**: each node is a raw
  `textarea` (edit layer) over a `contenteditable`/`MarkdownRenderer` display layer. Not CM6.
- Explicit per-note toggle via command/file menu calling **`leaf.setViewState({type: ...})` on
  the active leaf — public API, no monkey-patching**. (Automatic association is simply not
  offered; a leaf left in outline view is restored by workspace persistence.)
- `OutlineParser` does bidirectional md↔tree conversion; file I/O is manual
  `vault.read`/`vault.modify` plus a hand-rolled "anti-race-condition save queue".
- A five-module "isolation architecture" (view-state manager, command proxy, event delegator,
  runtime validator with periodic health checks) exists solely to keep the parallel editor
  from interfering with native Obsidian.

**What its costs demonstrate** (each one a predicted consequence of the custom-view route):

- **The conversion is lossy and normalizing — the anti-example for our isomorphism
  requirement.** The line-regex parser: forces tab indentation and `- ` markers on rewrite
  (ordered lists are parsed but re-serialized as bullets), globs *all* consecutive non-list
  content (headings, paragraphs, fences, tables) into single opaque blob nodes, misparses

input.question: How does the "Improve the style of your lists" (BetterListsStyles / list styling) feature work? What exact CSS does it inject, which selectors and CSS variables does it use, and how does it change list indentation width, bullet rendering, and `.cm-hmd-list-indent` / `.cm-indent` spans in CodeMirror 6 Live Preview? Also: how does the vertical indentation-lines feature (ListLines / VerticalLines) compute and render the lines — measured DOM rects or CSS?

content.content:
{"result":"The "Improve the style of your lists" (BetterListsStyles) feature in the `vslinko/obsidian-outliner` plugin primarily uses CSS to modify the appearance of lists in CodeMirror 6 Live Preview . It adjusts the margin of unordered list formatting elements and restyles the list bullet itself . The vertical indentation-lines feature (ListLines / VerticalLines) computes and renders lines by measuring DOM rects and dynamically creating HTML elements, rather than relying solely on CSS  .

## BetterListsStyles Feature

The "Improve the style of your lists" feature, referred to as `BetterListsStyles` in the prompt, applies specific CSS rules when the `.outliner-plugin-better-lists` class is active .

### Injected CSS and Selectors

The feature injects the following CSS:
*   It targets unordered list formatting elements within CodeMirror's Obsidian theme (`.cm-s-obsidian .HyperMD-list-line`) .
*   It sets a `margin-right` of `0.3em` for the `.cm-formatting-list-ul` class .
*   It styles the `::after` pseudo-element of `.list-bullet` to create a custom bullet appearance, setting its `width`, `height`, and `background-color` .

### CSS Variables Used

The feature uses the CSS variable `--text-muted` for the `background-color` of the list bullet .

### Changes to List Indentation Width and Bullet Rendering

*   **List Indentation Width**: The provided CSS primarily affects the `margin-right` of the unordered list formatting element, which can influence the spacing around the bullet . It does not directly change the overall indentation width of the list items themselves through these specific rules.
*   **Bullet Rendering**: The `::after` pseudo-element of `.list-bullet` is styled to render a custom bullet, which is a `0.4em` by `0.4em` square with a `background-color` defined by `--text-muted` .

### Changes to `.cm-hmd-list-indent` / `.cm-indent` Spans

The provided CSS for `BetterListsStyles` does not directly modify the `.cm-hmd-list-indent` or `.cm-indent` spans . However, the `outliner-plugin-vertical-lines` class, which is related to the vertical indentation lines feature, sets `content: none;` for the `::before` pseudo-element of `.cm-hmd-list-indent .cm-indent` . This effectively hides any default content that might be rendered by CodeMirror for these indentation spans when vertical lines are enabled.

## Vertical Indentation-Lines Feature (ListLines / VerticalLines)

The vertical indentation-lines feature, implemented by the `VerticalLines` class, computes and renders the lines by measuring DOM rects and dynamically creating HTML elements   .

### Computation and Rendering Mechanism

1.  **DOM Preparation**: The `VerticalLinesPluginValue` class creates two main DOM elements: a `scroller` (`.outliner-plugin-list-lines-scroller`) and a `contentContainer` (`.outliner-plugin-list-lines-content-container`) . These elements are appended to the CodeMirror editor's DOM .
2.  **Recalculation Trigger**: The lines are recalculated when the document changes, the viewport changes, geometry changes, or a transaction reconfigures the view . Recalculation is also scheduled when settings change .
3.  **Line Data Calculation**: The `calculate` method identifies visible lists within the editor's viewport . It then recursively traverses the list structure using the `recursive` method to determine the `top`, `left`, and `height` for each vertical line  .
    *   The `left` position is calculated based on the `coords.right` of the list's first line content start and a `rootLeft` context .
    *   The `top` and `bottom` positions are determined using `view.lineBlockAt` for the start and end offsets of the list, considering the visible ranges and zoom range .
    *   The `height` is derived from the `bottom` and `top` values, with an adjustment for siblings .
4.  **DOM Update**: The `updateDom` method dynamically creates `div` elements with the class `outliner-plugin-list-line` for each calculated line . It sets the `top`, `left`, and `height` styles of these elements based on the calculated `LineData` . The `scroller` and `contentContainer` styles are also adjusted to match the editor's scroll and content dimensions .
5.  **CSS Styling**: The appearance of these dynamically created line elements is controlled by CSS rules for `.outliner-plugin-list-line` . This includes `position: absolute`, `width`, `margin-left`, `margin-top`, `z-index`, `cursor`, and a `linear-gradient` for the background to create the vertical line effect .

Therefore, the vertical indentation-lines feature uses a combination of JavaScript to measure DOM rects and calculate positions, and then applies these calculated positions to dynamically created HTML elements which are styled with CSS   .

## Notes

The prompt mentions "BetterListsStyles" and "ListLines / VerticalLines" as features. The codebase directly references `outliner-plugin-better-lists` in `styles.css`  and has a dedicated `VerticalLines.ts` file . The `styles.css` file also contains CSS rules for `outliner-plugin-vertical-lines`  and `outliner-plugin-list-line`  which are directly related to the `VerticalLines` feature. Other files like `specs/features/EnterBehaviourOverride.spec.md`  and `src/operations/DeleteTillCurrentLineContentStart.ts`  are not directly related to the styling or rendering of lists and vertical lines, but rather to operational behaviors within the editor.

Wiki pages you might want to explore:
- [Drag and Drop Functionality (vslinko/obsidian-outliner)](/wiki/vslinko/obsidian-outliner#4.3)

View this search on DeepWiki: https://deepwiki.com/search/how-does-the-improve-the-style_dca07570-8efe-4d86-bd92-b9d42b2b353d
"}

## Results — Experiment 2a: guide lines via pixel-measured overlay

**Verdict: keep.** Branched off Experiment 1 (`experiment/decorations-2a-guides-overlay`).
All 8 corpus fixtures plus 4 real vault notes pass, both themes, screenshotted and visually
reviewed at pixel level (not just DOM-asserted) — see
`e2e/specs/51-guides-overlay.e2e.ts` (on the unmerged
`experiment/decorations-2a-guides-overlay` branch — 2a's code never merged), 43/43 e2e
tests green across the full suite (not just this spec). One ancestor-with-children gets one
continuous overlay `<div>` spanning from its first child's own line to its deepest
descendant's last line, positioned by *measuring* (`view.coordsAtPos`/`view.lineBlockAt`)
the ancestor's own already-rendered position rather than recomputing depth × unit —
obsidian-outliner's technique, applied to this project's universal (not list-only) tree.

**Real-vault finding, fixed on this branch (not a separate follow-up)**: a *list-item*
ancestor gets no guide of its own, deliberately. Our own real-vault comparison
(built-in indent guides only / both / ours only, screenshotted side by side) showed two
problems, both traced to the same cause: (a) with Obsidian's native "Show indent guides"
setting on, list nesting got visibly doubled lines; (b) even alone, our guides within a
list read as unevenly spaced, because native list nesting has its own internal per-level
width that our fixed unit doesn't match (the same native-hang mismatch Experiment 1 already
deferred rather than fight, now visible one layer up). Native indent guides already connect
one bullet precisely to the next *within* a list — there is no gap for a second mechanism to
usefully fill there. Fixed by having `computeGuides` skip pushing a guide when the anchor
node's `kind === 'list-item'`, while still including list-item subtrees in a *non-list*
ancestor's own span (a heading or paragraph bridging into a list still gets its guide,
reaching all the way through — only the within-list levels get none of their own). This
turns, e.g., the `deep-nesting` fixture (four levels, all list items) into zero guides at
all — entirely deferred to native — while `heading-then-list` keeps exactly one guide
(the heading's, spanning the whole list) instead of three.

**Deliberate deviation from the plan's literal wording**: the plan called for "a dedicated
`StateEffect`" for the out-of-band mode-toggle refresh. Dispatching a raw CM6 effect from
`main.ts` (application code, not a registered extension) has no path through Obsidian's
public `Editor` API — `EditorTransaction` exposes no `effects` field, and reaching into
`(editor as any).cm.dispatch()` is exactly the private-API surface this project's own
research already flags to avoid outside registered extensions
([03-obsidian-api-feasibility.md](03-obsidian-api-feasibility.md)). Used per-instance state
comparison instead (`ViewPlugin`/`StateField` each remember the outline-mode flag they last
saw and compare on every transaction — cheap, since it's just a boolean read, not a
reparse): functionally identical gate (`docChanged || viewportChanged || mode-just-toggled`),
zero private API. `main.ts`'s existing cursor-nudge dispatch (already public-API, unchanged)
still supplies the transaction that gives the comparison a chance to run.

**Code cost**: ~35 lines added to `decorate.ts` (`computeGuides`, a second tree walk),
~140-line addition to `decorations.ts` (a hand-rolled, debounced `ViewPlugin` reusing
`@codemirror/view`'s own exported `RectangleMarker` as a positioned-div factory, not CM6's
higher-level `layer()` helper — see the in-code rationale for why), ~20-line `styles.css`.

**Bugs found and fixed** (all three caught only by real e2e rendering/measurement — the
*pure* `computeGuides` unit tests were correct throughout; every bug was in the CM6
coordinate-system plumbing, exactly the kind of thing the postmortem warned unit tests
can't see):

1. **Guides rendered ~76px too high, caught by an e2e rect assertion, root-caused via live
   DOM diagnostics.** `view.lineBlockAt(pos).top/.bottom` are relative to `view.documentTop`
   (itself viewport-relative, moves with scroll) — not to the guide layer's own container
   origin (`scrollDOM`'s top-left, where the container's `top: 0; left: 0` anchors it). The
   two differ by a real, non-zero, confirmed-live constant (`.cm-content`'s own offset within
   the scroller). Fixed by converting through `documentTop` the same way `coordsAtPos`'s
   result already gets converted through a `getBase()`-style subtraction for the x-axis —

content.content:
# content-space-caret Specification

## Purpose

Defines which document positions the caret may occupy in outline mode, and how it gets
there. Gap lines and list-item marker prefixes are encoding chrome, not content, so they
are not addressable: motion keys skip them, and a placement that would land on one
resolves through OWNERSHIP — a gap belongs to the node above it, a marker to the line it
prefixes — rather than by nearest-position proximity.

Two mechanisms carry this, deliberately kept apart. **Motion** computes its target
directly from the parsed tree, so a keypress moves the caret to a legal position rather
than to an illegal one that is corrected afterwards. **Placement resolution** is the
backstop in the transaction filter, catching cursors from every other source — clicks,
selection collapses, and Obsidian's own unannotated dispatches — so the invariant holds
for gestures this capability never binds. Neither applies outside outline mode, where
caret behavior stays byte-for-byte native.

The scope is caret PLACEMENT, not editing. Where a caret may rest is this capability's
concern; what an edit at that position means belongs to `node-edit-enforcement`, and how
a non-empty selection expands belongs to `node-selection-enforcement`.
## Requirements
### Requirement: Only content positions are caret-addressable in outline mode
In outline mode, within the plugin's jurisdiction, the set of document positions the caret
may occupy SHALL be the union of every node's own content spans, TOGETHER WITH the entire
document preamble, TOGETHER WITH any PROVISIONAL POSITION a structural keypress has just
created. A blank gap line SHALL NOT otherwise be an addressable position. A list item's
marker prefix — its leading indentation, marker character, and any whitespace after it, the
span `contentBoundaryCh` identifies as non-content — SHALL NOT be
addressable, on the item's first line or as alignment whitespace on a continuation line. A
heading's `#` prefix and an atom's own lines ARE content and remain fully addressable.

**Provisional positions.** `outline-keyboard-grammar` defines a provisional position: the
blank line an accepted Enter or Shift+Enter leaves the caret on, holding the place where a
node or a continuation line materializes when text is typed. It is a gap line, and the caret
resting there is deliberate. The exception is narrow in exactly the way the rest of this
requirement is: it covers the transaction that CREATES the position, which is `plugin-own`
and already passes through untouched, and it does not make gap lines reachable by anything
else. A later gesture that moves the caret onto that same line resolves it like any other
gap line, and moving the caret away from it — or deleting it — triggers
`structural-history-integration`'s undo-on-abandon rather than leaving a caret behind.

This is stated rather than left implicit because the split operation has parked the caret on
a gap line since it shipped, which the previous wording — "a blank gap line SHALL NOT be an
addressable position" — read as forbidding. The behavior was never wrong; the requirement
was silent about the one case that needs it.

**Jurisdiction.** This property SHALL hold for positions produced by user gestures in
outline mode. Transactions classified `plugin-own` or `composition` SHALL pass through
untouched per `node-selection-enforcement`.

Transactions classified `programmatic` SHALL pass through untouched too, with ONE narrow
exception: an unannotated (`userEvent`-less), change-free transaction whose resulting range
is EMPTY and falls inside a list item's marker prefix SHALL have that cursor clamped to the
line's content start. Gap-line placements from such transactions are NOT corrected, and
non-empty ranges are never touched.

The exception exists because a marker clamp is not new — it predates this capability as
`node-edit-enforcement`'s `clampCursorToContent` and always applied to any cursor from any
source — while gap-line resolution IS new and is deliberately scoped to user gestures. It is
also load-bearing: Obsidian's own checkbox-widget mount dispatches an unannotated selection
change that puts the caret back on the marker, and without this the invariant has a hole
wherever any foreign unannotated cursor move lands.

Outside that exception, a caret placed by a `programmatic` transaction may rest on a
non-addressable position until the next user gesture moves it. The preamble — frontmatter
and any other content before the first node, where `nodeAtLine` resolves to nothing — is
outside the plugin's jurisdiction entirely: motion, placement, and extension there SHALL be
byte-for-byte stock.

The property SHALL be verified over generated documents, not only for the enumerated key
bindings.

#### Scenario: No user gesture reaches a gap line
- **WHEN** any arrow key, Home, End, mouse click, or selection collapse would place the
  caret on a blank gap line
- **THEN** the caret occupies a content position instead

#### Scenario: A structural keypress may leave the caret on its own provisional position
- **WHEN** Enter at the end of a paragraph, or Shift+Enter at the end of a list item, places

This is a key insight: in outline mode, the caret can never land inside a list item's leading indentation, since the marker prefix (indentation plus marker plus trailing space) is entirely non-addressable, and selection snaps to node granularity. That means the leading whitespace is already treated as chrome rather than content, which makes replacing it with a fixed-width widget or collapsing it visually much more justifiable.

I'm also thinking about the marker itself — whether to keep the native bullet but reposition it onto the guide column, or replace it entirely with a custom widget similar to how Obsidian restyles `.list-bullet` via CSS. The latter seems easier and more customizable through CSS variables and settings.

Before going further, I want to actually measure this empirically rather than theorize, so I should write a probe e2e spec. I need to check how fast the e2e harness runs, whether there's a cached build, and look at the wdio config for spec filtering, plus check git log for prior probe spec examples to follow an established pattern.

content.content:
# Obsidian List Threading CSS Implementation Analysis

## Overview
This gist provides CSS snippets that add visual threading lines to bullet lists in Obsidian's live preview and source view modes. The implementation uses CSS selectors targeting CodeMirror's HTML structure combined with pseudo-elements to draw lines.

## Core Selectors & Mechanism

The CSS relies on these key selectors:

- **`.HyperMD-list-line-N`** - Classes marking list items at nesting depths 1-6
- **`.cm-hmd-list-indent`** - The indentation pseudo-element container
- **`.cm-active`** - Marks the currently active/focused line
- **`:hover`** - Triggers hover-based threading display

Threading lines are rendered using **`::before`** and **`::after`** pseudo-elements on `.cm-hmd-list-indent`, with `position: absolute`, explicit width/height, and colored backgrounds to create vertical and elbow connector lines.

## Indentation Handling

The implementation uses **`var(--list-indent)`** CSS variable to dynamically calculate offsets:

> "using `--list-indent` variable to hopefully make the snippet more compatible with styles that alter it"

Offset calculations multiply `var(--list-indent)` by nesting depth:
```
calc(var(--list-threading-offset-extra, 2px) + var(--list-padding-inline-start-fix) + n * var(--list-indent))
```

## Indentation Format Caveats

The author explicitly warns about space-based indentation limitations:

> "the editor is inherently non-monospace, and various live-preview components use it in whatever way they like"

**Key caveat:** Tabs are strongly recommended. Space-based indentation (2, 3, 4 spaces) produces misaligned threading because:
- List indentation width doesn't match the `--list-indent` CSS variable reliably
- The implementation prioritizes wrapped text over images by default (configurable)
- Font-dependent rendering creates fractional character widths

Users employing spaces must manually adjust `--list-indent` values per indentation count (e.g., `39.5px` for 4-space indentation).

content.thinking:
This confirms that community CSS threading only works reliably with tabs, validating how difficult this really is in practice. The key question now is whether to measure native list geometry like obsidian-outliner's overlay approach, or to own it by normalizing the per-level step to our unit — the latter being what would actually get lists on par with headings and paragraphs, since if lists step by exactly our decor unit, the existing gradient guide mechanism would work unchanged.

This would also let the marker mechanism place bullets on the same columns, make alignment with same-depth siblings exact, let the ancestor trail work through lists without a second mechanism, and make indentation independent of tabs vs. spaces — a genuine outliner property like Logseq or Workflowy have. The cost is breaking the "byte-identical to outline-mode-off" invariant the spec treats as a hard requirement for pure lists, but that's a spec choice we made ourselves, so it could be deliberately amended rather than broken in passing — the real question is what that invariant's purpose was actually protecting against.

Once we own list geometry, the right invariant becomes "outline mode off stays byte-identical to stock" plus "outline mode on renders a consistent, unit-based outline." I'm weighing one candidate mechanism: replacing leading whitespace with a fixed-width widget sized to the indent level, which gives exact control regardless of tabs or spaces since it replaces the native indent markup entirely rather than fighting its width — though I need to check how this interacts with Obsidian's own mark decorations and widget buffer elements on those same ranges.

I'm also considering a second approach: zeroing out the native whitespace width via CSS and applying our own margin per line instead, though this raises questions about handling continuation lines correctly.

Pros are that it avoids introducing a new CM6 mechanism, relying purely on CSS and our existing per-line custom property. The downside is that collapsing the width could mess with caret coordinate calculations and potentially break Obsidian's own measurement of the hanging indent, since there are nested spans inside that Obsidian uses for that purpose.

I'm now weighing a third option: directly overriding the native padding and text-indent pairing per line.

Since whitespace is invisible, letting it render over the padding region costs nothing visually, which is elegant. The catch is that W needs to be measured per line, but unlike guide columns this measurement is simple and local with a stable fallback available. I'm also noting that text-indent only affects the first formatted line of a block, while continuation lines in CM6 are separate line elements, so this approach needs more thought for wrapped lines.

Widget replacement seems cleanest conceptually: if I control the rendered width of the indentation, Obsidian's own hang computation—which operates on rendered widths—should automatically line up with it by construction. I'm now questioning whether that's actually true, or whether Obsidian computes the hang some other way entirely.

Rather than guessing, I should just extract app.css directly from the Obsidian asar file — it's a simple format I can parse with a quick node script, and that would give me ground truth CSS instead of speculation.

I found something important: Obsidian 1.13 uses a public `--list-indent` CSS variable that controls tab-indented list steps, and each `.cm-indent` span has a min-width set to that same variable—meaning a full indent renders consistently whether it's a tab or spaces.

I also discovered the native indent guide is actually themeable through public variables like `--indentation-guide-width` and `--indentation-guide-editing-indent`, which default to 0/transparent when the setting is off—explaining why I measured it as invisible earlier. I want to track down the default values and where the "show indentation guides" setting actually sets them, since this reshapes my understanding significantly.

input.description: Find indent-unit/size and active guide selectors

content.thinking:
I notice Obsidian already marks the active indent span with its own distinct guide color and width — essentially its native equivalent of a position indicator for list levels, so that mechanism is already handled. I'm also calculating the list indent size: with `--indent-size: 4` and `--indent-unit: 0.5625em`, that works out to 2.25em per level.

At 16px base font, that's 36px — matching the measured step from Finding 3. I'm now digging into how `.cm-indent` spans get generated, tracing through the tokenizer logic to figure out whether the count is based on spaces-per-unit or tabs, since tab-indented lists seem to produce one `.cm-indent` per tab while space-indented ones seem to follow a different divisor.

This leads to a key realization: the inconsistent per-level step is purely an artifact of inconsistent source indentation. If a document uses tabs or a fixed 4-space unit consistently, every list level steps by exactly `--list-indent`, and since that's a public CSS variable, I could set it directly to control native list indentation precisely — since `tab-size` accepts a length value and `.cm-indent` uses matching min-width, both tab-indented and space-indented lists could be made to step uniformly by overriding this one variable.

But 2-space indentation remains the broken case: with only two raw spaces, there's no `.cm-indent` wrapper at all, so min-width can't rescue it — the measured bullet columns confirm this gap is real regardless of what I set `--list-indent` to.

This confirms that 2-space (and similarly odd) indented lists are inherently misaligned in Obsidian's Live Preview as stock behavior — four source spaces collapse into one `.cm-indent`, while leftover spaces render literally, so an outliner plugin would need to normalize this itself. I recall the project already integrates with CM6's public `indentUnit` facet to read the "Indent using tabs" setting, so I want to check how the plugin currently writes indentation for list items.

Looking at how the plugin writes indentation, I see two complementary paths forward: normalizing the rendered indent step so every list level maps to our unit regardless of source whitespace (which would fix 2-space documents), and leveraging Obsidian's own public CSS variables for list indent, guides, and bullets to align native rendering with our unit — a low-risk change with strong payoff for the common tab/4-space case. Now I want to examine the remaining CSS rules governing list line padding and text-indent.

I'm digging into Obsidian's CSS variables for list indentation—finding that `--list-indent` combines the indent unit and size to produce 2.25em, which controls tab-size and minimum indent width, while `--list-padding-inline-start` varies between live preview and other modes.

Bullet styling turns out to be entirely variable-driven too: size, radius, border, transform, and color are all controlled through CSS custom properties on `.list-bullet::after`, meaning custom bullet shapes like squares or chevrons require no plugin logic at all, just variable tweaks. I'm also noting how native indentation guides work, using a bordered pseudo-element positioned via margin based on another editing-indent variable.

I'm now tracing the active-indent highlighting mechanism, which uses separate width/color variables to distinguish the current indent level, and I want to check what sets the editing-indent variable to zero in certain contexts. I also spotted `--list-spacing` controlling vertical padding on list lines — this looks like exactly the spacing consistency gap the user flagged for our block lines. I should dig into the indent-size and indent-unit variables next to see how they connect to the indentation settings.

Now I want to set up an empirical probe to validate the app.css reading against a real running Obsidian and test candidate mechanisms — starting with a baseline geometry measurement across outline mode on/off using fixtures with tab, 4-space, and 2-space indented lists at multiple nesting levels.

For each line I'd capture bullet position, content-start x, indent widget counts and widths, computed padding on list formatting elements, tab-size, and the resolved CSS custom properties controlling indentation and guides.

Then I want to check whether native indent guides actually render in live preview given the setting — the CSS I read suggests guides might be unconditional in source view regardless of the toggle, which contradicts an earlier finding of 0px/transparent guides. This could be a version difference between Obsidian 1.12.7 and 1.13.4, since the indentation-guide variables might be new in 1.13, so I need to check which app version the test harness actually resolves to — this matters a lot for interpreting results. Finally I want to test whether overriding the list-indent CSS variable to match our unit is feasible.

I'm planning a CSS-only normalization test: giving the list-indent span an explicit computed width based on our own known indent level, then checking whether the bullet lands at the expected position, whether click/caret placement still works, and whether soft-wrap continuation stays aligned. If this works, it would mean we can control list geometry with just one CSS rule and a custom property we already compute — no measurement hacks needed, which would be a great outcome.

But I realize I need to be careful: the indent span only exists for nested items, not level-1 ones, and continuation lines carry different whitespace than the item's own leading indent, so the width formula would need to differ between a list item's first line and its wrapped continuation lines. I also need to account for the "nobullet" case separately.

I notice Obsidian already has a rule compensating continuation lines by padding them with the marker gap, which explains the mismatch I measured earlier — it adds a fixed amount that doesn't scale with wider markers like "10.". If I control both the indent span width and the marker width myself, I can align continuation lines exactly instead of relying on that fixed padding.

        hi = L['hmdIndent']['rect'] if L['hmdIndent'] else None

        st = L['style']
        print(f"  L{L['n']} {txt!r:28s} rect.l={rect['l']:7.2f} pad={st['padding-left']:>7s} mar={st['margin-left']:>7s} ti={st['text-indent']:>8s} tab={st['tab-size']:>6s}")

for k in ['tab-pure::off','tab-pure::on','sp4-pure::off','sp2-pure::off','sp2-pure::on']:
    show(k)
    print()
EOF

content.thinking:
I'm examining the measured widths of the list-indent spans, noticing the width equals the sum of its child `.cm-indent` elements' min-widths — confirmed by the 2-space case where the span width matches the raw space width plus any indent units.

The line's padding-left and negative text-indent create the native hanging indent, with padding-left equal to the rounded sum of indent width plus marker width — this appears to be computed and applied natively by Obsidian per line rather than through our own CSS, which matters for whether we can override it. I also notice the `.list-bullet` element is absent on the first line in the off-mode case but present in on-mode, which I want to dig into further.

So the padding actually comes before the bullet glyph, meaning even at level 1 there's a 12px indent before the dash appears — that's the `--list-indent-editing: 0.75em` value. Checking sp2, the bullets confirm it's broken as predicted, with level 2 only 8.38px further in and level 4 only 8.38px past level 3, while our decoration unit is 24px (1.5rem).

Even in the working tab case, native list levels step 36px while heading/paragraph levels step 24px — that mismatch is likely what's causing the perceived inconsistent spacing. Next I want to check the list-indent override, explicit width, guides, caret round-trip, and compare the kinds at each depth.

content.thinking:
Setting `--list-indent: 24px` on `.markdown-source-view` gives a decisive positive result: both tab and 4-space lists step by exactly 24px per level, matching the target unit, and Obsidian automatically recomputes the line's hanging indent to match.

Ordered lists behave the same way, but 2-space lists remain broken as predicted since 2 spaces don't register as a `.cm-indent`. So one public CSS variable solves unit-consistent indentation for tab/4-space documents essentially for free — that's the right approach to the whole problem.

Testing the alternative approach of setting width via a calculated level on `.cm-hmd-list-indent`, I find it actually works for tab and 4-space documents, computing 24/48/72px correctly across levels. But for 2-space lists the level calculation breaks down at deeper nesting — level 1 computes correctly but level 2 rounds incorrectly, giving 24px instead of the expected 48px.

Despite the width mechanism working, I notice the hang padding and text-indent values stay fixed at the level-1 value across all lines in this approach, unlike the first method where they tracked correctly — suggesting Obsidian re-measures the hang when a CSS variable changes but not when we directly override width via injected CSS.

Maybe it's not JS-measured per line at all—perhaps Obsidian sets text-indent/padding via a CSS custom property computed from measuring the marker, and my overflow:hidden rule created a new block formatting context that changed how that measurement walked the span, collapsing it to marker-width only.

But the real issue is whether the hang actually matters: it governs alignment of soft-wrapped continuation lines. With padding 23 and text-indent -23 on a level-3 item, the first row starts at 0 but wrapped rows land at 23px, while the actual content starts at 71px—so wrapped text would be badly misaligned under my CSS-width-override approach.

I'm now wondering whether E1's `--list-indent` value is genuinely measured or just computed via a CSS calc formula, so I want to check if padding-left is set as an inline style versus a stylesheet rule. There's also a possibility that CodeMirror 6 has some built-in mechanism I haven't considered yet.

Before chasing that further, I should just directly measure the inline style attribute and check the soft-wrap alignment results from E2, E3, and E4, along with the kinds-at-depth comparison and continuation baseline.

content.thinking:
I'm tracing through Obsidian's ViewPlugin logic that builds line decorations, extracting indent prefixes and estimating text width for lines outside tree regions to set negative text-indent styling.

The `updateDomInternal` function actually measures live rendered positions via `coordsAtPos`, clears inline styles, computes the real prefix width, caches it per line, and writes the final `textIndent`/`paddingInlineStart` values. This runs on doc changes, viewport changes, geometry changes, selection, focus, or tree updates, and there's also a MutationObserver watching the content DOM that triggers re-measurement. So the hang is really a live DOM measurement baked into inline styles with per-line caching — which explains why my injected CSS experiment produced inconsistent padding values across lines, since the measurement was re-triggered by the mutation but something about the cache or timing wasn't behaving as expected.

I'm now digging into why all lines showed the same pad value of 23 in that experiment, tracing through how the prefix width is computed from `coordsAtPos` and whether the prefix includes just whitespace or the marker too — testing against the `- l1`, `\t- l2` examples to see if the math checks out.

I realize this is a feedback loop issue — padding shifts content right, but clearing text-indent before measuring should force a reflow via getBoundingClientRect, so that part should be fine. Rather than keep speculating, I should just run another measurement pass with more instrumentation, capturing the inline padding value and checking soft-wrap behavior directly.

E1's approach works because changing the indent variable alters the rendered width, and the measurement correctly reflects that new width — the numbers confirm a clean linear relationship. E2's approach, using CSS width on the indent span, desyncs the measurement, likely because overflow:hidden turns the span into a block formatting context that throws off coordsAtPos. I should test E2 without overflow:hidden to see if it stays viable for the 2-space case.

I'm also weighing whether the 2-space case matters much at all, since Obsidian defaults to tabs and a user with tabs off and tab-size 2 would already get broken columns in stock Obsidian — normalizing the file's indentation would fix it but that's a document rewrite, outside the scope of a decoration layer. One idea is that since --list-indent also controls tab-size, setting it to match the document's unit would make tab-indented docs render perfectly.

For space-indented docs though, I realize the fix only works when showIndentGuide is on, since that's what creates the .cm-indent spans with their min-width; with it off, spaces render at natural width and tab-size has no effect — so there's a genuine dependency on that setting I need to verify against the E3-false data. Now it's clear: the hanging indent is a per-line inline style set by Obsidian's own measuring ViewPlugin, cached by line number and prefix text. It's stale in the C variants because the injected CSS didn't invalidate Obsidian's cache, which only re-measures lines when its own logic decides to.

Checking the minwidth variants confirms this — the padding values match the pre-injection measurements, not the new CSS. So any mechanism that changes the rendered prefix width must either apply via CSS variables already in effect before Obsidian measures, or somehow invalidate Obsidian's private per-line cache, which is fragile since it's only cleared on doc changes or similar triggers.

Given that risk, I'm settling on a safer strategy: rather than fighting the measurement loop, change the inputs it reads. Setting `--list-indent` to our spacing unit, scoped to outline-mode editors, should make tab- and space-indented lists (with guides on) step by our exact unit and let the hang recompute natively — though I need to watch for cases where indentation guides are off, or where this variable also affects rendered content like embeds and callouts within the editor.

Good, that confirms the variable resolves correctly at the point of use on `.cm-line`, inheriting from `.cm-content`.

For the residual 2-space/guides-off case, I'm weighing options: forcing indent guides on isn't viable, matching `--indent-size` to the tokenizer won't work since it's hardcoded to 4, but replacing the leading whitespace with a widget decoration could work cleanly since it changes what Obsidian actually measures. Otherwise I could just document the limitation and offer a normalization command as a fallback.

The widget-replacement approach seems worth probing further — replacing the whitespace span on list lines with a widget sized to `level × unit` should be real inline content that Obsidian's measurement picks up correctly, though I need to watch for interactions with widget buffers, atomic ranges, Obsidian's own indent mark decorations, and caret behavior. Checking how Obsidian's hang plugin actually measures position, it calls `coordsAtPos` at the end of the marker prefix, which should still work fine even with a replace widget covering the whitespace before it.

content.thinking:
The wrapped line only returned one rowTop since getClientRects on a block element gives a single rect, so I couldn't directly measure the wrapped row's start position. But the hang mechanism's negative text-indent combined with matching padding means wrapped rows naturally start at the content column, so the soft-wrap alignment checks out.

Checking the other fixtures: outline mode was off for the depth1-kinds test so those are native values only; nested lists inside callouts worked correctly (pad stepped from 61→49), though I should visually verify that scoping the indent variable to `.cm-content` doesn't unexpectedly affect rendered markdown inside embeds; and tasks with folding also indent properly (66→54). Now I'm testing a bullet restyle with custom size, radius, color, and editing indent to see how the marker width responds.

Shrinking `--list-indent-editing` from 0.75em to 0.2em pulled the marker width down from 23.42 to 14.62 and moved the bullet from 12 to 3.2, confirming this variable controls the pre-marker gap and that the hang follows it — a solid public lever, with bullet appearance fully variable-driven. Setting it to 0 would put a level-1 bullet right at x=0, meaning I could align the bullet exactly with a marker-icon column. Now I want to look at active indent tracking.

This is a real scoping constraint for per-editor overrides.

content.thinking:
Soft wrap is confirmed working correctly — wrapped rows align exactly under the item's own text at the content column, so the native hang mechanism adapts properly to the new list-indent value without extra work. I'm also checking a callout with a nested list, where the rendered list item shifted position, confirming that list-indent also governs the callout's nested ordered list styling.

The sp2 fixture exposes the real problem: 2-space indented lists land one level short and misaligned at every depth, confirming they're unusable without normalization first. I also found a leak where applying the probe CSS globally causes non-outline notes to render their lists at the same 24px steps, meaning the CSS must be explicitly gated to outline mode only — likely by scoping the list-indent variable to lines or content tagged via our line decorations rather than applying it globally.

Testing this further, a tab on a continuation line that isn't itself a `HyperMD-list-line` falls back to the default tab-size rather than inheriting `--list-indent`, since that custom property only applies to list-line elements. That explains the misalignment I saw — continuation content lands at 18px while the list item's own content starts at 23.42px.

With mode off, the plugin's own decorations disappear but our probe CSS stays active, confirming the gating works correctly. I'm also verifying that `--indentation-guide-editing-indent: 0` applies properly when set on `.cm-content` since `.cm-indent::before` is a descendant selector — probe 3 confirmed this by shifting guides from 61.6 to 48.

Now I'm checking that `--list-padding-inline-start` also works when scoped to `.cm-line.to-decor-list`, since `.cm-formatting-list-ul/ol` is a descendant of the line too. Before writing the plan, I need to settle whether to keep native indentation guides for list levels or draw custom ones — native guides are free and include the active-indent highlight, but they're tied to the user's own "Show indentation guides" setting and color variable, which could conflict with our own styling.

Drawing our own guides via the existing gradient would stay uniform with block guides and work regardless of that setting, but it requires extending `computeLineGuides` to include list-item ancestors, which is a straightforward change. The tricky part is that `.cm-indent`'s min-width, which makes 4-space documents render at unit width, only exists when the native setting is on — so I can't just disable that setting outright, I need another way to suppress the native guide visually while keeping its underlying spans intact.

But that still leaves a gap: if the user has the setting off entirely, those spans never exist, so space-indented docs collapse back to their raw width. That's a real dependency I need to surface — either detect the vault's indent-guide config and adapt, or build a separate mechanism for handling space-indentation independent of that setting, like a replace-decoration widget over mismatched leading whitespace or a normalization command.

I'm leaning toward probing the decoration-widget approach since it's the only purely rendering-based fix, which means I need to inject a CM6 extension and check whether I can reach `@codemirror/view` from within Obsidian's runtime, since Obsidian marks CM packages as external and resolves them itself.  If that works, I could register a test extension via a state effect dispatch, though it might be simpler to just note this as a fallback and validate it during actual implementation rather than building a throwaway probe now.

But the project's discipline calls for validating uncertain mechanisms before planning around them, and the widget approach is the genuinely unclear piece, so it's worth probing cheaply. I'm also reconsidering whether a CSS-only approach could survive Obsidian's hang measurement for the space-indent case — since the earlier failure was due to cache staleness, having the CSS present in styles.css from the start rather than injected later might avoid that issue, so I want to test a width-override variant on the indent class to check.

I'm also thinking through the cache invalidation logic: since the width depends on a per-line custom property tied to whitespace, text changes should properly invalidate Obsidian's cache, but I need to consider edge cases like reparenting where the level changes without a whitespace change — though that still counts as a document change, so it should be fine.

I want to test both the CSS-width override in a fresh editor and the widget approach together in one probe, since the key question is whether the fresh-editor CSS override produces a correct hang. For the widget test I'll need CM6 classes, so let me check the esbuild externals setup first.

content.thinking:
N2 couldn't actually be tested since the widget mechanism relies on Obsidian's module loader rather than Node's require, so I'll flag it as the one unvalidated fallback needing a hook inside the plugin itself. Meanwhile N1's CSS width check in a fresh editor confirms the geometry is correct, with the expected measurements lining up properly.

But digging into the wrapped-row data, I notice the soft-wrap alignment is actually broken — the hang indent stuck at 23px instead of picking up the new content column, meaning Obsidian's measurement of the prefix width isn't reflecting the forced CSS width on the inline-block span. I'm trying to trace why: it could be that Obsidian clears the text-indent/padding before measuring and that throws off the layout, or there's some re-measurement step triggered by a threshold check that's using stale values.

More likely culprit: the per-line cache is skipping lines whose cached text matches, but since `--probe-level` gets set by `tagLevels()` only after the initial render, the first measurement happens when the width is still zero, so it caches the marker-only width (23px) and never invalidates once the real width is applied later. Then after an edit, CM6 recreates the DOM nodes and wipes out the inline style property entirely, explaining why the measured width dropped to 0 for every line.

So this probe is inconclusive — a real implementation would set the level via `Decoration.line` attributes, which persist from the very first render, so Obsidian's measurement should see the correct width from the start. That's plausible but still unverified, and the real question is whether Obsidian's hang-measurement logic runs after our decoration's attributes are applied during the same DOM update cycle.

Since both are line attributes updated together, it likely does measure the final width correctly, though there's a caching wrinkle: Obsidian's cache is keyed by line number and prefix text, not by our custom property, so changes to our level without a text change could leave stale measurements — though line-number shifts from document edits probably already force cache invalidation elsewhere. I'm concluding this approach is promising but needs a real validation spike in the plugin itself rather than a throwaway probe, which gives me a concrete first task for the plan.

For the space-indented case specifically, I consider whether letter-spacing or word-spacing tricks on the indent whitespace could force Obsidian's own quantizer to see a full unit without touching the source — but word-spacing only applies between words, and letter-spacing would need to know the doc's indent width (2 vs 4 spaces) to compute correctly, which feels fragile. I'm leaning toward the conclusion that the cleanest general fix is just enforcing consistent indentation in the source itself.

Breaking down the actual remaining gaps: tab-indented docs work perfectly with `--list-indent`, 4-space docs with indent guides on should also work, but 4-space docs with guides off and 2/3-space docs remain broken since they fall back to natural width. I want to check what `showIndentGuide` defaults to in Obsidian's config, and also reconsider whether the `.cm-indent` spans are always created or only gated behind that setting — if they're conditional, that changes the scope of what's fixable.

The extension that builds indent marks must be conditionally included based on whether the setting is on, since the measurement showed zero spans when it's off. I'm confirming this matches the observed behavior: guides off means no spans, which means space-indented content renders at natural width regardless of CSS tricks. I'm also ruling out `tab-size` as a lever since it only affects tabs, not spaces, and checking whether `--indent-size` offers any path forward.

I should verify the `showIndentGuide` default and gating logic, and also check whether these CSS variables even exist in older Obsidian versions like 1.12.7, since the test harness's earliest installer version is 1.5.8 and these features might be too recent.

List the list-related CSS variables it documents (e.g. --list-indent, --list-spacing, --list-marker-color, --list-bullet-size, --list-bullet-radius, --list-bullet-border, --list-bullet-transform, --list-bullet-end-padding, --list-numbered-style) and any indentation-guide variables.
